tip: 'Kollega' pluralizes to 'kollegor', then 'kollegorna' for the colleagues.
'Enkelbiljett' is a one-way ticket, from 'enkel' (single); a return is 'tur och retur'.
'Dagis' is the everyday word for daycare: 'lämnar barnen på dagis' = drops the kids at daycare.
'Åka' is the go-by-vehicle verb: 'åker Öresundståget' = take the Öresund train.
'Vill' means 'want', not English 'will': 'jag vill lära mig' means I want to learn, not I will learn.
'Istället för' is the fixed phrase for instead of: 'te istället för kaffe'.
Frequency uses 'gånger' plus 'i veckan': 'tre gånger i veckan' = three times a week.
'I morse' = earlier this morning (already past); don't mix it up with 'i morgon' = tomorrow.
'Sina' is the plural of 'sin' (one's own), pointing back to the subject: 'hjälper sina grannar'.
'Somna' means fall asleep (the change), while 'sova' means be asleep: 'innan de somnar'.
Possessives agree with the noun: neuter 'besök' takes 'mitt', so 'mitt första besök'.
'Som' is the all-purpose relative pronoun – it replaces who, which, that.
Adjectives after 'är' agree too: neuter 'barnet' makes 'glad' become 'glatt', so 'barnet är glatt'.
'Liten' is wildly irregular: definite 'lilla', plural 'små'. Here 'vår lilla fest' = our little party.
Adverbs normally add '-t' to the adjective: 'vacker' becomes 'vackert', so 'sjunger vackert' = sings beautifully.
Swedish keeps the verb in second place, so fronting 'i Sverige' puts 'äter' ahead of the subject 'man': 'i Sverige äter man'.
Swedish keeps the present with 'sedan' (since) for ongoing actions: 'studerar ... sedan hösten' = have been studying since autumn.
A definite noun with an adjective usually needs a front article too: 'den andra butiken' = the other shop.
One big verb group forms the past with '-te' or '-de': 'undersöker' becomes 'undersökte' = examined.
'Skynda sig' (to hurry) needs its pronoun to match the subject: with 'vi' it becomes 'skynda oss'.
'Sin' means 'his/her own', pointing back to the subject: 'till sin familj' = to his own family.
'Inte' (not) comes right after the verb in a main clause: 'jag förstår inte' = I don't understand.
'Samma' paired with 'som' means the same as: 'samma skola som ditt barn' = the same school as your child.
'Varandra' means each other: 'spelar schack mot varandra' = play chess against one another.
For travel in general drop the article: 'åker buss' = go by bus, versus 'tar bussen' for a specific one.
'Går att' means can be done: 'går inte att öppna' = cannot be opened.
A definite noun with an adjective normally takes a double marker: 'det stora trädet', both 'det' and '-et'.
'Under' can mean 'during' for a time span: 'under lunchen' = during lunch.
After 'som' a profession takes no article: 'arbetar som lärare' = work as a teacher.
'Gammal' is irregular in the superlative: 'äldsta' = oldest, so 'min äldsta syster'.
